Seven out of the eight Ivy League schools are [Colonial Colleges](/wiki/Colonial_colleges "Colonial colleges"): institutions of higher education founded prior to the [American Revolution](/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"). Cornell, the exception to this commonality, was founded immediately after the [American Civil War](/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). These seven colleges served as the primary institutions of higher learning in [British America](/wiki/British_America "British America")'s [Northern](/wiki/New_England "New England") and [Middle Colonies](/wiki/Middle_Colonies "Middle Colonies"). During the colonial era, the schools' faculties and founding boards were largely drawn from other Ivy League institutions. Also represented were British graduates from the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), the [University of Oxford](/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), the [University of St. Andrews](/wiki/University_of_St._Andrews "University of St. Andrews"), and the [University of Edinburgh](/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh").

The influence of these institutions on the founding of other colleges and universities is notable. This included the Southern public college movement which blossomed in the decades surrounding the turn of the 19th century when Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia established what became the flagship universities of their respective states. In 1801, a majority of the first board of trustees for what became the [University of South Carolina](/wiki/University_of_South_Carolina "University of South Carolina") were Princeton alumni. They appointed [Jonathan Maxcy](/wiki/Jonathan_Maxcy "Jonathan Maxcy"), a Brown graduate, as the university's first president. [Thomas Cooper](/wiki/Thomas_Cooper_(American_politician,_born_1759) "Thomas Cooper (American politician, born 1759)"), an Oxford alumnus and University of Pennsylvania faculty member, became the second president of the South Carolina college. Main article: [2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii § District 2](/wiki/2006_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Hawaii#District_2 "2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii")

On September 23, Hirono ran to represent [Hawaii's 2nd congressional district](/wiki/Hawaii%27s_2nd_congressional_district "Hawaii's 2nd congressional district") in the House of Representatives after incumbent [Ed Case](/wiki/Ed_Case "Ed Case") chose not to seek another term. The Democratic primary was crowded and very competitive. There were ten candidates, seven of whom served in the [Hawaii Legislature](/wiki/Hawaii_Legislature "Hawaii Legislature"). Hirono's advantage was that she was the only candidate who had held statewide office and, as a result, had the most name recognition. She led in fundraising, helped by the endorsement of [EMILY's List](/wiki/EMILY%27s_List "EMILY's List").[[25]](#cite_note-25) She won with a plurality of 22% of the vote. State Senator [Colleen Hanabusa](/wiki/Colleen_Hanabusa "Colleen Hanabusa") finished second with 21%, 845 votes short of Hirono.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In the general election Hirono defeated [Republican](/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") State Senator [Bob Hogue](/wiki/Bob_Hogue "Bob Hogue"), 61%–39%.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

Main article: [2008 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii § District 2](/wiki/2008_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Hawaii#District_2 "2008 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii")

Hirono won reelection to a second term with 76% of the vote.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Main article: [2010 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii § District 2](/wiki/2010_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Hawaii#District_2 "2010 United States House of Representatives elections in Hawaii")

Hirono won reelection to a third term with 72% of the vote.[[30]](#cite_note-30)
